payload.stem: A hurricane destroys a large share of a country's factories but not its workers or its farmland. Compared with the production possibilities curve before the storm, which statement is correct?

options.text: The economy moves to a point inside the old curve, but the curve itself stays where it was.
options.why: Treats the damage as an inefficiency; destroyed factories lower the maximum possible output, so the curve shifts inward.

options.text: The economy moves down along the same curve, because the country now produces fewer goods.
options.why: Confuses a loss of productive capacity (a shift) with a choice of a different combination on the same curve.

options.text: The curve shifts outward, because rebuilding factories will create many jobs.
options.why: Mixes the later effect of rebuilding with the immediate loss of capital; the loss of factories reduces capacity.

options.text: The curve does not change, because workers and farmland are unaffected and the curve depends only on labor and land.
options.why: Ignores capital as a resource; any lost resource reduces the feasible output.

options.text: The curve shifts inward, because the economy's stock of capital has shrunk, so some earlier combinations of output are no longer attainable.
options.why: Losing capital reduces the feasible output combinations, so the whole curve moves inward (especially for goods that use capital).

payload.stem: A country's production possibilities curve shows capital goods on the vertical axis and consumer goods on the horizontal axis. A new technology raises the output per worker in consumer goods only. Which change in the curve is most likely?

options.text: The curve shifts outward in a parallel way, because better technology raises the maximum of both goods by the same amount.
options.why: Assumes a parallel shift; a technology specific to one good changes only that good's intercept.

options.text: The curve does not change, because technology changes the price of the good rather than the possible output.
options.why: Treats technology as a price effect; technology changes the feasible output and therefore the curve.

options.text: The curve pivots outward along the consumer goods axis, while the maximum quantity of capital goods stays the same.
options.why: Technology that improves only one good raises the maximum of that good and leaves the other intercept unchanged, so the curve pivots.

options.text: The curve shifts inward, because producing more consumer goods leaves fewer resources for capital goods.
options.why: Confuses a movement along the curve with a shift; reallocating resources does not move the curve itself.

options.text: The curve pivots outward along the capital goods axis, because the new technology frees up resources for capital goods.
options.why: Pivots the wrong intercept; the technology changes output per worker in consumer goods only.

payload.stem: A bakery has already purchased a $500 oven that cannot be resold. Baking one more batch of bread adds $90 to revenue and costs $70 in ingredients and labor. Which statement about the next batch is correct?

options.text: The bakery should bake it only if the oven cost is divided evenly among all batches it will ever bake.
options.why: Allocating a sunk cost across batches still makes it irrelevant to the marginal decision.

options.text: The bakery should not bake it until the batch's revenue covers the $500 oven.

payload.stem: When the price of printers falls, the quantity of ink cartridges that consumers buy at every price rises. Which statement correctly identifies the relationship between printers and ink cartridges?

options.text: They are normal goods, because demand for ink cartridges changes when the price of printers changes.
options.why: Normal and inferior describe the response to income, not to another good's price.

options.text: They are substitutes, because the demand for ink cartridges moves in the same direction as the price of printers.
options.why: Reverses the sign rule for cross-price effects; check whether the demand moves with or against the other good's price.

options.text: They are inferior goods, because the demand for ink cartridges changes in a way that depends on the price of printers.
options.why: Inferior goods are defined by income, not by a price change of a related good.

options.text: They are unrelated goods, because the price of printers should affect only the quantity of printers.
options.why: Confuses a movement along the demand curve for one good with a shift in demand for a related good.

options.text: They are complements, because the demand for ink cartridges moves in the opposite direction to the price of printers.
options.why: Complements have a negative cross-price elasticity because the goods are used together.

options.why: Treats a subsidy like a tax; a subsidy lowers sellers' costs and shifts supply right.

options.text: The tax raises the price buyers pay and lowers the quantity traded, while the subsidy lowers the price buyers pay and raises the quantity traded.
options.why: A tax shifts supply left (higher price, lower quantity), and a subsidy shifts supply right (lower price, higher quantity).

options.text: Neither changes the quantity traded, because the government only moves money between buyers and sellers.
options.why: Ignores the incentive effect; both policies move the quantity away from the market equilibrium.

options.text: The tax lowers the price buyers pay and the subsidy raises it, because the government gains from the tax.
options.why: Reverses the price effects; a tax shifts supply left, raising the buyers' price.

options.text: Both reduce the quantity traded, because government intervention always reduces trade.
options.why: Assumes any intervention reduces trade; a subsidy raises the quantity traded.

options.text: The model assumes only two goods and a fixed set of resources and technology, while a real economy produces many goods and its resources and technology change over time.
options.why: Simplifying assumptions (two goods, fixed resources and technology) make the model easy to use but limit how closely it matches a real economy.

payload.stem: Which statement correctly compares producer surplus and consumer surplus at a competitive equilibrium?

options.text: Producer surplus equals total revenue, while consumer surplus equals total spending minus total revenue.
options.why: Equates surplus with revenue; surplus subtracts costs or willingness to pay from the price.

options.text: Producer surplus is the difference between the price and the buyers' willingness to pay, while consumer surplus is the difference between the price and the sellers' cost.
options.why: Swaps the two definitions; consumer surplus uses buyers' willingness to pay and producer surplus uses sellers' costs.

options.text: Producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the demand curve, which is the same as consumer surplus.
options.why: Describes total surplus; each surplus is a separate triangle bounded by the price line.

options.text: Both surpluses equal zero at the equilibrium, because the market clears there.
options.why: Confuses market clearing with zero gains; only the marginal unit has zero surplus.

options.text: Producer surplus is the difference between the price sellers receive and their minimum acceptable price, while consumer surplus is the difference between buyers' maximum willingness to pay and the price paid.
options.why: Both are net gains from trade measured against the market price, one for sellers and one for buyers.

payload.stem: Which of the following correctly describes average fixed cost (AFC) as output increases in the short run?

options.text: AFC equals marginal cost, because both are costs of one unit.
options.why: Marginal cost is the cost of an added unit; AFC is the fixed cost per unit of all units.

options.text: AFC is U-shaped, because of diminishing marginal returns.
options.why: Describes ATC and AVC; AFC has no rising portion.

options.text: AFC rises when output rises, because more machines are needed.
options.why: In the short run fixed cost does not change with output, so AFC cannot rise with Q.

options.text: AFC stays constant, because fixed cost does not depend on output.
options.why: Total fixed cost is constant, but the cost per unit falls as it is spread over more units.

options.text: AFC falls continuously, because the same total fixed cost is spread over more units.
options.why: AFC = TFC / Q with TFC constant, so it declines as Q rises (spreading overhead).

payload.stem: A man invests $50,000 of his savings in a food truck instead of keeping it in an account that pays $3,000 a year. He pays $18,000 for ingredients and fuel. Which of the following is an implicit cost of operating the business?

options.text: The wages the business pays to a part-time employee.
options.why: Wages paid to an employee are payments to another party, so they are explicit costs.

options.text: The $18,000 paid for ingredients and fuel.
options.why: Ingredients and fuel are paid for with money, so they are explicit costs.

options.why: The invested money is a stock; the yearly implicit cost is the return it could have earned.

options.text: The truck's total revenue.
options.why: Revenue is a benefit, not a cost of any kind.

options.text: The $3,000 of interest he gave up.
options.why: An implicit cost is the value of a resource the owner supplies, measured by the best alternative use; it involves no payment to another party.

payload.stem: Which statement correctly compares average variable cost (AVC) and average total cost (ATC) as output increases?

options.text: The gap between ATC and AVC widens as output rises, because fixed cost grows with output.
options.why: Fixed cost is constant in the short run, so the gap per unit shrinks.

options.text: AVC is always above ATC, because variable cost is larger than total cost.
options.why: Total cost includes variable cost, so ATC is at least AVC.

options.text: The gap between ATC and AVC is marginal cost, so it changes with each unit.
options.why: The gap is average fixed cost, not marginal cost.

options.text: ATC and AVC have the same minimum quantity, because both are U-shaped.
options.why: ATC reaches its minimum at a larger output than AVC because AFC keeps falling after AVC begins to rise.

options.text: The vertical gap between ATC and AVC equals average fixed cost, so the gap narrows as output rises.
options.why: ATC = AVC + AFC, and AFC falls with output, so the gap between ATC and AVC shrinks.

A regulator requires the firm to charge the lowest price at which the firm just breaks even (price equal to average total cost) while serving as many customers as possible. What price must the firm charge?

options.why: Sets the price equal to average fixed cost at the larger quantity.
Price equals ATC where 18 - 1Q = 4 + 33/Q, which has roots Q = 3 and Q = 11; the larger quantity gives the price $7.
Charges the unregulated monopoly price, where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
Uses the smaller of the two quantities where price equals average total cost, which serves fewer customers.
Charges the price at the demand curve's vertical intercept.
